2907.dq: Stress is mostly found in penultimate syllables, although it can also be found in the antepenultimate and in the last syllable of a word (as in some of the examples above).
2907.dloc: Sec. 5.2 'Stress', pp. 68-70; restated in ch. 6 'Summary and conclusions', p. 77.
2907.heavy: 'heavy' is not defined for Yamalero; the tendency is quoted from the Sikuani analyses (Queixalos 1985a; Kondo 1985c; Mosonyi, Guevara & Guevara 2000): 'if the antepenultimate syllable of a word is heavy, it will also be stressed. 2907.prule: Stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive): segmentally identical minimal pairs differ in stress alone (pe.'pa 'half' vs 'pe.pa 'pure'; 'ke.xe.wa 'one' vs ke.xe.'wa 'nearby'; ba.'ha.ra 'yes' vs 'ba.ha.ra 'no'). No assignment rule is stated: 'The rules of stress assignment have not been defined yet.' Majority pattern penultimate; antepenultimate and final also occur.
2907.srule: Not mentioned in Ginebra 2022, sec. 5.2 'Stress' pp. 68-74 and ch. 6 p. 77 (only 'primary stress' is named, in connection with stressed suffixes; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described)

2907.tone: Not tonal. Correlates unsettled: 'High pitch and vowel length seem to be the two best indicators', intensity in a few words (Praat figs 15-18: daütjü, nekona, peha, nühü); syllable-timed, no vowel reduction. 2910.dq: When two minor syllables occur in a word, the first minor syllable always functions as the negative marker, while the second is an inherent part of the lexical base. This creates a fixed Minor–Minor–Major template. ... In these cases, both syllables remain unstressed and phonologically reduced.
2910.dloc: Ch. 4, sec. 4.2.3 'Words with minor syllables', p. 19.
2910.prule: No word-stress rule. Six contrastive lexical tones borne by every major syllable. The only stress statement is Matisoff's sesquisyllable definition adopted for the language: the major (full, tone-bearing) syllable is 'fully stressed' and the preceding minor syllable(s) (V or C+schwa, obligatorily open, toneless) are 'unstressed' and 'phonologically reduced', including both syllables of the NEG-prefix + minor + major template. Nothing on relative prominence among the major syllables of compounds (up to five syllables), no instrumental stress data.
2910.quote: [p.19, sec. 4.2.3 Words with minor syllables] The term sesquisyllable, which is derived from the Latin sesqui- meaning “one and a half,” was coined by Matisoff (1973) to describe a phonological unit characteristic of many Southeast Asian languages. It consists of a major syllable which is fully stressed, vowel rich, and tone bearing, preceded by an unstressed minor syllable or presyllable ((Matisoff, 1973, p. 86). When two minor syllables occur in a word, the first minor syllable always functions as the negative marker, while the second is an inherent part of the lexical base. This creates a …
2910.loc: Ch. 4, sec. 4.2.3 'Words with minor syllables', p. 19; supporting sec. 4.1.1 p. 14, sec. 4.1.2 p. 16, sec. 5.3 'Tones' p. 29, sec. 5.3.1 'Tone sandhi' p. 31.
2910.idn: Pounyiu dialect of Gongvangpounyiu Naga (ISO 639-3 npg); speakers from Pounyiu Nuakzian (new Pounyiu village) and Pounyiu Nuakgong (old Pounyiu village); the other dialect group, Gongvang, is not described (a named variety of the language); data: Language of Lahe and Hkamti townships, Sagaing, Myanmar; data recorded…
2910.tone: Tone language: six contrastive lexical tones on major syllables (Table 17 header lists 11, 33, 55, 31, 51, 14: three level, two falling, one rising); the rising tone is restricted to checked syllables (voiceless stop, glottal stop, glottalized glide codas); tone sandhi in compounds (bidirectional, regressive, progressive). Minor syllables carry no contrastive tone but show pitch variation the author flags for future research (possibly conditioned by the following major syllable's tone). On stress the thesis says only that the major syllable of a sesquisyllable is 'fully stressed' and the minor syllable(s) 'unstressed' and 'phonologically reduced' (definition from Matisoff 1973 applied to the NEG+minor+major case); 'stress' occurs nowhere else in the thesis; no prominence rule among major syllables.

2912.dflt: All-light words are parsed into LL iambs from the left, so every even-numbered underlying vowel is stressed and the odd-numbered ones syncopate; primary stress on the head of the penultimate foot (e.g. /ənənəwək/ (ənə)(nəwək) -> 'nenˌwek 'men'); a leftover final light syllable stays unfooted (/ənənəw/ -> ˈnene 'man').
2912.prule: Word-level, quantity-sensitive iambic system stated over underlying (pre-syncope) forms: syllables are parsed left-to-right into iambic feet (LL, LH, or a lone H; heavy = syllable whose nucleus is a long/'strong' vowel); every foot head bears (secondary) stress; feet are grouped right-to-left into left-headed cola and primary stress goes to the head of the rightmost colon, i.e. to the head of the penultimate foot when there are two or more feet, to the only foot head otherwise. Surface citation forms given: ˈnene 'man' /(ənə)nəw/, 'nenˌwek 'men' /(ənə)(nəwək)/, ˌnesh'naˌbé 'Indian' /(ənə)(ʃəna:)(bɛ:)/, ˌneshˌna'bémˌwen 'Indian language' /(ənə)(ʃəna:)(bɛ:)(mowən)/. 2912.srule: Secondary stress on the head of every iambic foot other than the one bearing primary stress; feet are parsed left-to-right over underlying (pre-syncope) vowels and are weight-sensitive (a long-vowel syllable is heavy: LL, LH, H): 'Secondary stress falls on the heads of the iambic feet'. 2913.heavy: Heavy = syllable with a long vowel (दीर्घ); secondarily the akshara/syllable carrying a geminate consonant (व्यंजन-द्वित्व), stated literally as stress 'on' the doubled consonant. A long vowel outranks a closed (CVC) first syllable (condition 4: CVC.CVV -> final). Short-vowel (ह्रस्व) open syllables are light.
2913.dflt: Not stated: no light-light example; folio 108 treats stress as otherwise free / emphatic.
2913.prule: Disyllabic words only (the only length treated). (1) 'When disyllabic words are long' stress falls on the first syllable (मोठो; the Lodhanti/Marari examples घाती, मूता likewise have two long vowels, so 'long' is read as both syllables long: an inference from the examples, not the wording). (2) Short first vowel + long second vowel -> stress on the second (मुंगी, उड़ीद). (3) A geminate consonant attracts stress: the text literally puts the stress on the doubled consonant itself ('ट तथा क पर बल' for चोट्टिन, डुक्कर), i.e. on the akshara containing the geminate; which of the two syllables is meant is not resolved. (4) In three-akshara disyllables with a short first vowel and a long final vowel (phonetically CVC.CVV: झुनकी, हटका, मुंगसा) the final syllable is stressed, so a long vowel outranks a closed first syllable. No default for words without a long vowel or geminate; stress is otherwise described (folio 108) as free and used for meaning contrast / emphasis.

2914.dq: At most one high (H) tone per phonological word (cf. Hyman 2014). [fn. 1] ... Regarding all-Ø words, we found no evidence of a prominent syllable, i. e., no phonetic correlates of “stress” (pitch, intensity, length).
2914.dloc: Postprint p. 2 fn. 1 (§1) and §5 p. 29 (all-Ø words).
2914.heavy: Not a stress rule; for the tone system the source states: 'there can only be one heavy syllable (CVV, CVC, CVG) per word; (ii) this syllable must bear a H tone' (weight-to-tone; fn. 37 'If a syllable is heavy, it must bear a H').
2914.prule: No word stress. Word prosody is a privative, culminative but non-obligatory /H/ tone: at most one H per phonological word, position lexically stored and synchronically unpredictable (in H-nouns 68% penult, 23% final, 9% antepenult, reflecting the Portuguese etymon's stress); monosyllabic nouns must bear H; verbs (with five exceptions) and most African-origin nouns are toneless and show no prominent syllable. Weight-to-tone: the single heavy syllable a word may have (CVV, CVC, CVG) must carry the H. The authors for phonetic and phonological correlates of stress (vowel/consonant asymmetries, consonant strengthening, post-tonic reduction effects, clash resolution, prominence in all-Ø words) and found none.
2914.srule: None: the source finds no word stress of any degree — 'Another place to seek evidence for stress is in subordination and rhythmic effects. As seen in (27), neither is found in Lung’Ie'; 'No clash resolution for adjacent H tones'; 'All-Ø words do not show any kind of prominence' (H tone is culminative: at most one per phonological word).

2917.prule: Word stress is culminative and falls on the final syllable of the prosodic word (monosyllables stressed; di- and trisyllables final-stressed; all other syllables unstressed; words have at most three syllables; compounds keep final stress, e.g. ko.ˈta 'treinta'). Weight plays no role; duration is the proposed correlate. One stated morphological exception: the 3sg possessive suffix -ʔa is unstressed and stress stays on the root-final syllable ([tso.ˈʔa.ʔa] 'su bigote', [tʲo.ˈʔa.ʔa] 'su cocinera', p. 83). The stressed syllable licenses the oral/nasal contrast, morphological contour tones and laryngealized vowels.

2918.prule: Penultimate stress by default. Lehmann-Nitsche, the fieldworker who recorded the language from speakers in 1915-16, states in his manuscript vocabulary that the accent falls on the penultimate syllable unless specially marked otherwise; the editors (Malvestitti & Orden 2014: 41) paraphrase this as 'es usual la acentuación en la anteúltima sílaba' and note that secondary stresses and stresses departing from this pattern are recorded systematically. Orden 2018 (working from the same written records) describes instead a hedged tendency to initial stress in isolated lexemes and characterises stress functionally as culminative and demarcative; but every example she gives for initial stress is disyllabic (initial = penult) and every polysyllabic or affixed form she cites (da'süka, panǘ-nüp, küjǘ-kja, ahwai-úkach, agáye, kaláuhna, kuchá-chaw, and ajuaí-kia with monosyllabic -kia/-kja) is penultimate, so her data conform to Lehmann-Nitsche's default. No weight condition is mentioned by any source.
2918.srule: Secondary accents exist in Lehmann-Nitsche's transcriptions: the editors say his notation records 'de forma sistemática y detallada la realización de los acentos secundarios'. Their placement is not stated by Lehmann-Nitsche or the editors, and Orden 2018 (Sec. 3.4) does not mention secondary stress.

tn.quote: Se parte de la hipótesis de parentesco entre las lenguas chon y el günün a yajüch, idioma que se habló en el norte de la Patagonia y región pampeana. Hasta donde se conoce, el günün a yajüch no tenía tonos a nivel fonológico. El proto-chon, en cambio, habría poseído dos tonos fonológicos, uno alto y otro bajo (Viegas Barros, 2022) … no hay tono a nivel fonológico en otras lenguas de la Patagonia con las cuales los idiomas chon estuvieron en contacto (yagan, kawésqar, günün a yajüch, mapudungun), cuando lo normal en las lenguas del mundo es que el tono sea un rasgo típicamente areal.
tn.translation: We start from the hypothesis that the Chon languages are related to günün a yajüch, a language that was spoken in northern Patagonia and the Pampas region. As far as is known, günün a yajüch had no tones at the phonological level. Proto-Chon, by contrast, would have had two phonological tones, one high and one low (Viegas Barros 2022) … [why] there is no tone at the phonological level in other languages of Patagonia with which the Chon languages were in contact (Yagan, Kawésqar, günün a yajüch, Mapudungun), when normally in the world's languages tone is a typically areal feature.

2919.heavy: 'a syllable with a long vowel' (rule 2); 'diphthongs are, however, not necessarily equal to long vowels'. Closed syllables are not named as heavy; the suffix-created closed penult of legángal (< légal + -ngal) is attributed to the 'heavy' class affix, not to syllable structure.
2919.dflt: antepenult in polysyllables of purely short syllables (rule 6, hedged 'many'); penult in all disyllables (rule 4) and in adjectives, adverbs, numerals except 6-9 and 1st-conj. finite verbs (rule 5)
2919.prule: Accent ('tone syllable') falls within a right-edge two-syllable window (penult or antepenult). A syllable with a long vowel attracts the accent (diphthongs do not necessarily count as long); if a word has two long syllables the one nearer the end takes it. Without a long vowel: penult in all disyllables and in adjectives, adverbs, numerals (except 6-9) and 1st-conjugation finite verbs; antepenult in 'many' polysyllables consisting only of short syllables. Ultima accent is rare (contracted negatives, the greeting kisiyé).
2919.srule: Not mentioned in Reichardt 1876, Ch. V 'The Accentuation' sect. 14, pp. 14-17: the section places a single 'tone syllable' per word and describes no secondary or rhythmic accent.

vnotes: Source ambiguous: tonal vs morphological: the cited set makes Punu a five-tone language with no stress rule in any modern work (-> tonal, the record's value), but Bonneau 1940, the work cited for the rule, does state a word-accent placement ('L'accent se place sur la syllabe racine', kept on the root under suffixes, with 'appui de la voix' as well as pitch) which, read as stress, is the catalog's 'morphological'. Bonneau's own definition of the accent as half pitch ('élévation de la tonalité') and half force leaves me unable to say which the source states.
2923.dq: 1° Dans chaque mot pounou, il y a au moins une syllabe accentuée.
2923.dloc: Bonneau 1940 p.136, section 'II. Accentuation', points 1°-4° (Persée page scan of p.136). Tomba Moussavou 2007 p.80 and conclusion; Tomba Diogo 2015 p.27 and fn.36.
2923.prule: Bonneau 1940: every word has at least one accented syllable; the 'accent' (defined as a raising of pitch plus a reinforcement of the voice) falls on the root syllable, which is the penult in simple words (Rŭ-ga 'come', du-săl-a 'feather'); it stays on the root syllable under the suffixes -ila, -ulu, -una, -unu, -ena (Rŭg-ila, i-tsăn-unu, u-kŏb-ena); verbs derived with -anga, -ungu, -esena, -usunu accent the penult instead (Rug-ă-nga); nouns with an incomplete C-V root accent the noun-class prefix (Bŭ-ta 'gun', dĭ-tu 'leech'). All later descriptions (Yukawa 2005; Tomba Moussavou 2007; Tomba Diogo 2015 after Kwenzi Mikala 1990) treat Punu as a lexical-tone language (extra-high, high, low, rising, falling) and give no stress rule.
2923.srule: Bonneau 1940 p.136, point 4°: in verbs of four syllables with the (main) accent on the penult, a lighter accent falls on the first syllable (Rŭg-il-ă-nga 'come often for'); stated only for this word shape.

2923.tone: Tomba Moussavou 2007 p.80: 'Yipunu is a tone language, which means that tones have a distinctive function.' Five tones listed (extra high, high, low, falling, rising); §3.4.3.3 gives the lexical pair bukùlu 'kind of vegetable' vs bùkulu 'genealogy'. Same page: 'The existing phonological and phonetic descriptions of Yipunu briefly discuss aspects of stress and word division in Yipunu'; conclusion: 'Yipunu urgently needs the phonological and phonetic investigation on stress, word division, etc.' Tomba Diogo 2015 p.27: 'Comme certaines langues bantoues, le yipunu est une langue à tons, on en compte précisément 5' (after Kwenzi Mikala 1990: 299-306), quoting Bonneau's accent sentence second-hand; fn.36 reports Rekanga (2006) as holding that the so-called supra-high tone is a falling contour whose vowel is slightly lengthened 'sous l'effet de l'accent'. Yukawa 2005 marks verb forms for H/L ('accent' in his terminology = tone) and states that Punu verbs have lost the inherited tonal-class opposition; no stress placement given. Bonneau's 1940 'accent' explicitly merges pitch ('élévation de la tonalité') with force and is the only placement statement in any reachable source.

2926.dq: Kemaloh Lun Bawang stress is not contrastive and appears, from the available data, to usually fall on a word’s final syllable. ... With potential confounding factors such as lengthening of word-final vowels and boundary tones factored out, the reasonable conclusion to adopt, until further work can confirm or refute it, is that Lun Bawang has word-final stress.

2926.prule: Non-contrastive word stress on the final syllable (ultima), quantity-insensitive, for words of two or more syllables; the antepenult of longer words is clearly unstressed. Author's conclusion p. 55: 'Lun Bawang has word-final stress.'

2927.dq: [p.46] The phonological word is defined as the rank which functions as the unit of the intonation group and whose structure is stated in terms of syllable. In Pwo Karen, a phonological word has only one main (strong) stress. The stress is placed on the last syllable of a phonological word.

2927.heavy: Primary stress is not weight-conditioned: it is positional (final). Syllable type governs only the non-final syllables' secondary vs zero stress (minor syllable C(C)VT = weak stress; presyllable Cə with neutral tone = no stress), and presyllables/minor syllables are barred from final position, so the final, stressed syllable is always a full tone-bearing syllable.
2927.prule: Fixed final. Each phonological word ('stress group') carries exactly one strong (primary) stress, on its last syllable; that syllable is always a 'major' syllable (full C(C)V + tone). Stress is positional and predictable, hence unmarked phonemically. Words are one to three syllables long; examples (p.67) kə'si 'horse', pə'kɔ 'mosquito', ˌpʰɛ'laiʔ 'monkey', tʰə lə'məʔ 'to be happy', kə ˌjɯ'pʰɛ 'gibbon'.
2927.srule: Weak (secondary) stress on every non-final minor syllable (full vowel + tone), marked [ˌ]; zero stress on non-final Cə presyllables (neutral tone). Placement is by syllable type, not rhythm: disyllables are z.'s or ˌw.'s, trisyllables z.z.'s or z.ˌw.'s (p.67), e.g. [ˌpʰɛ ˈlaiʔ] 'monkey', [kə ˌjɯ ˈpʰɛ] 'gibbon' vs [kə ˈsi] 'horse', [tʰə lə ˈmaʔ] 'to be happy'.

2927.tone: The variety is tonal: major and minor syllables each carry a tone (p.60: 'The structure of the minor syllable in Pwo Karen is C(C)VT'; p.54: the major syllable takes 'a tone'), presyllables carry 'the neutral tone' (p.68), and p.70 lists 'consonants, vowels and tones' as the three phoneme classes; the 'Five contrastive tonemes' line at p.45 belongs to the ch. 2 literature review of the author's 1993 Sangkhlaburi (Eastern Pwo) study, not to the Lamphun analysis. 2928.tone: Kato 2022 (Kyonpyaw dialect): four tones on full syllables, low-level [11], high-level [55], falling [51], checked [ʔ51] (checked tone has the pitch of the falling tone and is treated as both a tone and a final glottal stop); atonic /Cə/ syllables have no tone, are written without tone marks and are 'pronounced short and weak'. Kato 1995 (same dialect, 'Kyonbyaw'): three tonemes plus atonic /Cɤ/ syllables that never occur utterance-finally and cannot occur singly; tone alternation in numerals before classifiers (/lɤ̀/ 'one' > /kɤ-/); onset-tone co-occurrence restriction. Neither source uses 'stress' or 'accent' for Western Pwo. Kato 2021 (Typological profile of Karenic languages, LLMSEA ch. 18, author preprint) describes the same structure for Eastern Pwo as 'atonal syllables, which are phonetically unstressed and short' and sesquisyllabic words 'composed of the unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable', adding 'In PK and SK, the minor syllable in a sesquisyllabic word never has a tone'; that is the only prominence statement, and it is minor-syllable weakness, not a stress-placement rule.

2931.heavy: A light syllable contains only a single mora, i.e., only one of the five short vowels /a/, /e/, /i/, /o/ or /u/. A heavy syllable contains two morae. These two morae can be made up of a single long vowel (/aː/, /eː/, /iː/, /oː/, /uː/), which can be thought of as two adjacent vowels of the same type.... They can also, however, be made up of two non-identical vowel sounds occurring adjacent to each other, where the second vowel is higher than the first. In these cases, they make up a falling diphthong. 2931.prule: Words are parsed into bimoraic (moraic) trochees aligned to the right edge; the leftmost foot is the head, and primary stress falls on its first mora. No foot may split a syllable, so heavy syllables (long vowel or falling diphthong) are stressed on their first mora and attract the foot. Result: 2-mora words initial; 3-mora words on the penultimate mora (the middle light syllable, or the first mora of a final heavy syllable), but on the first syllable when it is heavy; 4- and 6-mora words on the first mora; 5-mora words on the first mora (first foot left-aligned, middle mora unfooted) unless the second syllable is long, in which case that syllable is stressed. Net effect: primary stress always lies on the first or second mora of the word.
2931.srule: One secondary stress, invariably on the penultimate mora, in words of at least four morae falling into at least three syllables; at least one (often more than one) unstressed mora separates it from the primary, so intermediate feet are unstressed. tn.quote: The Arakanese tones have similar realizations to those in Burmese: heavy: /ˋ/ high intensity; falling contour, generally fairly high Fo, breathy phonation; level: Ø low intensity; level contour, generally fairly low Fo, normal phonation; creaky: /ˊ/ creaky voicing, slightly falling contour, high Fo (stop-final): /ʔ/ short duration; very high Fo, final stop and no juncture voicing following. Some words have creaky tone in Burmese, but heavy tone in Arakanese, or less frequently vice versa.
tn.cite: Bradley, David. 1985. Arakanese vowels. In Graham Thurgood, James A. Matisoff & David Bradley (eds.), Linguistics of the Sino-Tibetan area: the state of the art, 180-200. Pacific Linguistics C-87. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C87.180.
tn.note: Burmese-type tones on full syllables: heavy (high falling, breathy), level (low), creaky (high, slightly falling); stop-final a fourth type, no tonal opposition. Schwa syllables toneless; no stress.

2933.heavy: 'hierarchy of syllable strength': strong (C)V1(C) > (C)V2C > (C)V2 > (C)V3C > weak (C)V3, 'V1 stands for the vowel [ɐ],V3 for the vowel [ə], and V2 for all other vowels' — i.e. a syllable with [ɐ] (orthographic <aa>) is strongest whatever its coda; among the other full vowels a closed syllable outranks an open one; schwa ([ə], orthographic <a>) syllables are weakest, closed schwa above open schwa.
2933.dflt: First syllable: 'If syllables have equal strength, stress is assigned to the first one' ([ˈpoŋo], [ˈkoku], [ˈkuro], [ˈənə], [ˈtubu], [ˈbene]). OPD 1999 p. 2 gives this default as the whole rule: 'Stress normally falls on the first syllable. Short functional words like <a > 'the, a' and <aa > 'past tense' are not stressed.'
2933.prule: Unbounded, prominence-driven: primary stress goes to the strongest syllable of the word on a five-step scale (C)ɐ(C) > closed syllable with any other full vowel (C)VC > open full-vowel syllable (C)V > closed schwa syllable (C)əC > open schwa syllable (C)ə; if several syllables tie, the first (leftmost) is stressed, so words of uniform syllable type are initially stressed. Examples: [liˈmɐnə] 'his hand', [ˈɐkɐkur] 'story', [weˈlɐr] 'like'; [məˈgo] 'stale', [kəˈbur] 'play', [ˈbukə] 'walking stick'; [ˈteŋlik] 'my brother', [miˈnoŋ] 'decoration', [kəˈnom] 'swallow', [mələˈlər] 'picture'; [ˈpoŋo] 'explode', [ˈkuro] 'pot', [ˈənə] 'his (food)'.
2933.srule: Secondary stress on every second syllable in both directions from the primary-stressed syllable: 'Secondary stress falls on every second syllable either way from the syllable which carries the primary stress' — [ˌmələˈlər] 'picture', [ˌtenəˈlik] 'his brother', [ˈɐkɐˌkur] 'story' (only trisyllables exemplified).
